what_it_does: Processors can be slowed by branches — decision points in a program where it could go one of two ways — especially when the outcome is hard to predict, causing the processor to stall while it waits to find out. A known trick is to run a lightweight "helper thread" in parallel that races ahead and pre-resolves these hard branches before the main thread reaches them. The problem is that one hard-to-predict branch can depend on the outcome of another hard-to-predict branch, so the helper thread itself gets stuck guessing. This paper introduces a system called Phelps (Predicated Helper Threads) that avoids the guessing problem by simply running the helper code for every possible branch outcome at the same time, using a technique called predication, then recording the results and letting the main thread pick the right answer. A special bookkeeping scheme ensures that when the first branch resolves, the main thread correctly uses only the results that correspond to the actual path taken.
